person.name: E._T._A._Hoffmann
person.summary: Ernst Theodor Amadeus Hoffmann (born Ernst Theodor Wilhelm Hoffmann; 24 January 1776 – 25 June 1822) was a German Romantic writer of fantasy and gothic horror, as well as a jurist, composer, music critic, and illustrator. His tales, including “The Nutcracker and the Mouse King,” “The Sandman,” and “The Golden Pot,” were central to German Romanticism and later inspired works such as Tchaikovsky’s ballet The Nutcracker and Offenbach’s opera The Tales of Hoffmann.

events.title: Birth in Königsberg
events.description: Ernst Theodor Wilhelm Hoffmann (later known as Ernst Theodor Amadeus Hoffmann) was born on 24 January 1776 in Königsberg, Prussia, into a family of jurists. He was the youngest of three children of barrister, poet, and amateur musician Christoph Ludwig Hoffmann and his wife Lovisa Albertina Doerffer.

locations.name_historic: Königsberg, Kingdom of Prussia (now Kaliningrad, Russia)

events.title: Parents separate and Hoffmann is raised by maternal relatives
events.description: Around 1778 Hoffmann’s parents separated. His father moved to Insterburg with Hoffmann’s elder brother, while his mother remained in Königsberg, where Hoffmann was brought up by his unmarried maternal aunts Johanna Sophie and Charlotte Wilhelmine Doerffer and their brother Otto Wilhelm Doerffer in a strict pietistic household that he later recalled as uncongenial.

locations.name_historic: Königsberg, Kingdom of Prussia (now Kaliningrad, Russia)

events.title: Education at the Burgschule in Königsberg
events.description: Between 1781 and 1792 Hoffmann attended the Lutheran Burgschule in Königsberg, where he made good progress in the classical curriculum. During these years he developed notable talent as a pianist and occupied himself with drawing and early literary experiments, including part of an unfinished novel titled "Der Geheimnisvolle".

locations.name_historic: Königsberg, Kingdom of Prussia (now Kaliningrad, Russia)

events.date_note: Year when he is noted as attending some of Kant's lectures
events.title: Begins university studies and attends Immanuel Kant’s lectures
events.description: In 1792 Hoffmann, together with his close friend Theodor Gottlieb von Hippel the Younger, attended some of Immanuel Kant’s lectures at the University of Königsberg. The exposure to Kantian philosophy and the intellectual milieu of Königsberg formed part of his early education and helped shape the critical and speculative tendencies that later surfaced in his literary work.

locations.name_historic: University of Königsberg, Königsberg, Kingdom of Prussia (now Kaliningrad, Russia)

events.title: Sent to Glogau after scandal over infatuation with Dora Hatt
events.description: By 1794 Hoffmann had become enamored of Dora Hatt, a married woman and his music pupil, ten years his senior. After her family protested his attentions, an arrangement was made in February 1796, with his hesitant consent, to secure him a post in Glogau in Prussian Silesia, effectively removing him from the situation and redirecting him toward a legal career in the provinces.

locations.name_historic: Königsberg, Kingdom of Prussia (now Kaliningrad, Russia)

events.title: Early provincial legal career and first efforts as a composer
events.description: From 1796 Hoffmann worked as a clerk for his uncle and guardian Johann Ludwig Doerffer in Glogau. After passing further legal examinations he visited Dresden, where the paintings of Correggio and Raphael deeply impressed him. In 1798 he moved with his uncle to Berlin, his first experience of a large city, and there attempted to establish himself as a composer by writing the operetta "Die Maske," which he sent to Queen Luise of Prussia in hopes of patronage.

events.title: Service in Prussian provinces and growing artistic ambitions
events.description: From June 1800 to 1803 Hoffmann served in various Prussian provincial posts in Greater Poland and Masovia, including Posen. Living away from family supervision for the first time, he acquired a reputation for a "dissolute" lifestyle by contemporary standards, yet he continued to draw, compose, and write, further developing his artistic ambitions alongside his legal duties.

events.title: Marriage to Mischa (Maria Thekla Michalina Rorer) and move to Płock
events.description: In 1802 Hoffmann married Mischa (Maria or Marianna Thekla Michalina Rorer, née Trzcińska) in Posen. Soon afterward he was transferred to Płock in New East Prussia, a move he regarded as an exile. There he coped with professional frustration and isolation by intensifying his writing and musical composition, experiences that later informed the melancholy and irony in his fiction.

events.title: Begins diary and gains first literary recognition with "Der Preis"
events.description: On 1 October 1803 Hoffmann began a personal diary during his difficult years in Płock. Around this time he published an essay on the theatre in Kotzebue’s periodical "Die Freimüthige" and entered a dramatic competition in the same journal with his play "Der Preis" ("The Prize"), about a play-writing contest. Although no entry received the prize, Hoffmann’s work was singled out for praise, marking one of his first public literary successes.

events.title: Appointed to a post in Warsaw
events.description: At the beginning of 1804 Hoffmann obtained a new administrative post in Warsaw, then under Prussian rule. On the journey he passed through his native Königsberg, where he met one of Dora Hatt’s daughters for the last time; he would never again return to his birthplace. The Warsaw appointment initiated what he later regarded as the happiest period of his life, immersed in a lively Polish and German cultural milieu.

events.title: Napoleonic occupation of Warsaw and loss of Prussian post
events.description: On 28 November 1806, during the War of the Fourth Coalition, Napoleon’s troops captured Warsaw, costing Hoffmann and other Prussian officials their positions. The bureaucrats divided the treasury and fled; in early 1807 Hoffmann’s wife and young daughter returned to Posen while he remained in Warsaw, fell seriously ill, and then, after refusing to swear allegiance to the French, was compelled to leave the Duchy of Warsaw. By June 1807 he had visited his family in Posen and returned to Berlin, resolving to pursue work as an artist and writer.

locations.name_historic: Warsaw, Duchy of Warsaw (now Warsaw, Poland)

events.title: Bamberg years: theatre work, music criticism, and first major fiction
events.description: On 1 September 1808 Hoffmann arrived in Bamberg with his wife to work as theatre manager. Although intrigues soon cost him that position, he remained in Bamberg, serving as stagehand, decorator, playwright, and private music teacher. He became a respected music critic for the "Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung," writing influential essays on Beethoven, and introduced his alter ego figure Kapellmeister Johannes Kreisler in its pages. In 1809 his story "Ritter Gluck" appeared, a tale of a possible encounter with the long-dead composer Gluck that marked his literary breakthrough. Around this time he adopted the pen name E. T. A. Hoffmann, stating that the "A" honored Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart.

locations.name_historic: Bamberg, Electorate/Kingdom of Bavaria, Holy Roman Empire/Kingdom of Bavaria

images.caption: Illustration of Kapellmeister Johannes Kreisler, Hoffmann’s fictional alter ego who first appeared in his music criticism and stories.

events.title: Moves to Dresden and Leipzig as opera director amid war
events.description: On 21 April 1813 Hoffmann accepted Joseph Seconda’s offer to serve as musical director for his opera company and left Bamberg for war-torn Saxony. He reached Dresden on 25 April, then struggled to travel to Leipzig because of military operations in the War of the Sixth Coalition. In May his family was trapped in Dresden during the destruction of the bridges and subsequent fighting, and later they endured the bombardment and Battle of Dresden. Hoffmann continued his work with Seconda’s orchestra, commuting between Dresden and Leipzig as the military situation allowed.

events.title: Publication of "Nachtstücke" consolidates his reputation
events.description: In 1817 Hoffmann published the two-volume collection "Nachtstücke" ("Night Pieces"), which included some of his most influential tales of the macabre and fantastic, such as "Der Sandmann" ("The Sandman"). Issued in Berlin by the Realschulbuchhandlung, the work helped secure his standing as a leading author of German Romanticism and a master of gothic horror.

images.caption: First edition of E. T. A. Hoffmann’s two-volume collection "Nachtstücke" (1817), published in Berlin.

events.title: Death in Berlin
events.description: E. T. A. Hoffmann died in Berlin on 25 June 1822 at the age of 46 after a long illness that progressively paralyzed him. At the time of his death he was both a senior jurist in the Prussian legal system and one of the most celebrated authors of the Romantic movement, known for his uncanny tales and innovative blending of music, law, and fantasy.

images.caption: Grave of E. T. A. Hoffmann in Berlin, marked by a simple headstone.
